title: The CAIO Mandate
subtitle: From technology leader to enterprise AI executive
summary: Define the CAIO role, its decision rights, its relationship to the CEO/CIO/CTO/CDO/CISO, and the operating outcomes the role is accountable for.

lessons.title: What a CAIO actually owns
lessons.body: Define the CAIO's decisions, peer boundaries, operating cadence, and first-year scorecard. Work through a customer-assistant example and draft your own decision rights.

lessons.title: Your transition map
lessons.body: Assess what you know and what you can prove. Translate past leadership into CAIO evidence, rank the gaps that matter, and build a 90-day plan with reviewed artifacts.
resources: NIST AI Risk Management Framework Core

lessons.title: Executive stakeholder architecture
lessons.body: Map decision rights across executives, design the forums that move work, resolve a data-and-vendor disagreement, and write an escalation and board-reporting path.

quiz.q: A CAIO charter gives the CDO consent authority over source-data quality and engineering ownership of integration reliability. A stock-replenishment assistant passes integration tests, but duplicate product IDs make one warehouse's recommendations unreliable. The CDO withholds consent for that warehouse; the other warehouses have passed their quality gates. What recommendation best preserves the charter and useful delivery?
options: Propose release across warehouses with extra engineering sampling, treating passed integration tests as sufficient evidence for the current scope.
Ask the CDO to take integration ownership during remediation, then request one combined quality-and-reliability approval for every warehouse.
Propose release for the qualified warehouses and a joint data-and-engineering repair plan before requesting consent for the excluded warehouse.
Hold every warehouse until the shared dataset is repaired, treating the withheld consent as an enterprise-wide block despite separate quality results.
quiz.explanation: Consent applies to the source-quality issue in its stated scope, while engineering still owns the system repair and reliability evidence. A scoped release preserves that authority and uses the qualified evidence; integration tests alone do not answer the CDO's quality concern.

quiz.q: An assistant pilot reduces average handling time by 20%, but reopened cases rise from 5% to 11%. Eligible-case coverage and staffing are unchanged. What is the strongest recommendation for the first-year scorecard review?
options: Hold expansion and investigate whether errors and rework offset the measured time reduction.
Expand and report the time reduction as realized value while tracking reopenings separately.
Continue expansion but revise the target to combine handling time and reopening rate into one score.
Stop measuring handling time and judge the pilot solely by the reopened-case rate.
quiz.explanation: Reopened cases are a countermeasure for the claimed speed benefit. The increase makes expansion premature because faster initial handling may create additional work or harm; both measures should remain visible.

quiz.q: A business unit wants to expand an internal read-only assistant to customers and allow it to change account details. The monthly portfolio review approved its original pilot budget. Which next review is most appropriate?
options: A portfolio review focused on incremental benefit because the original pilot already passed release.
A procurement review focused on vendor capacity because the underlying model will stay the same.
An adoption review focused on training customers because the internal users already accepted the workflow.
A release review of the new audience and write authority against fresh evidence and operating controls.
quiz.explanation: Audience and autonomy changes alter exposure even when the model remains unchanged. The release review must examine representative evaluation, permissions, fallback, monitoring, and accountable approval for the proposed scope.

quiz.q: A prospective CAIO can design evaluation and finance plans but has no reviewed decision evidence in either. In the next 90 days, they can chair an evaluation decision for a customer pilot with a risk reviewer, or draft a finance memo without access to a finance reviewer. The customer launch is due in eight weeks; portfolio budgeting is six months away. Which development priority is best supported?
options: Start finance, because the wider capital mandate outweighs the lack of a reviewer before the budget cycle.
Start evaluation, using the imminent decision and reviewer to demonstrate judgment on the current launch risk.
Divide time equally, producing two draft artifacts even if neither reaches a reviewed decision in the quarter.
Start general CAIO study, postponing both artifacts until the candidate can claim comparable experience in each.
quiz.explanation: The evaluation opportunity combines imminent consequence, a weak evidence base, and access to a real decision and challenger. Finance remains important, but its later deadline and missing reviewer make it a less effective first evidence sprint under these conditions.

quiz.q: A candidate writes an evaluation plan, has a domain expert critique it, revises the cases, and issues a reasoned pilot recommendation. It is a clearly labelled fictional exercise with no deployment or measured follow-up. On the lesson's evidence scale (2: credible design; 3: specialist-reviewed artifact; 4: led a decision or deployment with measured results and follow-up), which entry is strongest?
options: Level 2 for the evaluation work; fictional use cases cannot provide evidence beyond an independently prepared design.
Level 4 for evaluation leadership; the revised recommendation counts as a decision even without observed operating results.
Level 3 for the reviewed evaluation artifact; seek a live decision with measured follow-up to establish level 4 evidence.
Level 3 for deployment leadership; specialist review establishes delivery ownership although the system remains fictional.
quiz.explanation: The evidence establishes a reviewed artifact and documented judgment, which fits level 3. Fictional work can produce useful reviewed evidence, but it cannot establish live deployment ownership or the measured results and follow-up required for level 4.

quiz.q: Privacy must consent before customer transcripts go to a vendor; retention and training terms remain unresolved. Procurement may negotiate terms but cannot grant privacy consent. Both a local redacted test of real transcripts and a vendor test of wholly synthetic transcripts are already authorized. Which two-week plan best tests usefulness on the real workflow while respecting delegated authority?
options: Defer both authorized tests; sales owns the benefit, procurement and privacy resolve terms, and sales resumes discovery after the two-week review.
Upload redacted customer transcripts under procurement's contract authority; sales owns the benefit, privacy checks terms, and the group reviews results in two weeks.
Defer customer upload and test only synthetic vendor examples; sales owns the benefit, procurement and privacy resolve terms, and the group reviews results in two weeks.
Defer customer upload; sales owns the benefit, procurement and privacy resolve terms, and sales runs the authorized local test before the two-week review.
quiz.explanation: The local real-transcript test is authorized and provides more direct workflow evidence than synthetic examples alone. The plan also preserves privacy's consent authority over vendor upload; procurement's negotiation role does not transfer that authority.

quiz.q: One AI committee is becoming a bottleneck because it debates funding, architecture, release evidence, and urgent incidents in the same monthly meeting. What redesign best follows the lesson's stakeholder approach?
options: Give separate forums defined decisions and packets, with a named incident path and escalation authority.
Keep one committee but increase membership so each function can approve its own portion during the meeting.
Delegate every decision to business sponsors and let the committee review quarterly summaries of their choices.
Create separate forums by executive title and require each forum to sign off every AI initiative.
quiz.explanation: Forums work when organized around decisions such as investment, design, release, and incident response. More members or repeated signoffs preserve the queue, while blanket delegation can bypass control owners' authority.

quiz.q: A board packet says a support assistant should improve enterprise service, based on a supervised pilot in one unit. Controls for wider deployment are designed but untested. What should the CAIO change before presenting the funding request?
options: Present the pilot's percentage gain as the enterprise forecast, then cover limitations in the technical appendix.
State the tested population and supervision, distinguish proposed controls from results, and request a bounded next stage.
Replace the benefit figures with model benchmarks so directors can compare vendors without narrow pilot assumptions.
Remove the funding request until all units have been tested, then return with a single enterprise result.
quiz.explanation: The board needs a decision supported by the actual evidence and its limits. A bounded next stage can buy missing evidence; neither extrapolating a narrow pilot nor substituting benchmarks establishes enterprise value or proven controls.

homework: Write a 2-page CAIO charter for a 5,000-person company. Include mission, decision rights, interfaces with CIO/CTO/CDO/CISO, first-year outcomes, and what the CAIO explicitly does not own.
